summary:
Put the values in a hash set, and only start counting at a value whose predecessor
`value − step` is **not** in the set: that value is the head of a chain. Walking forward from
heads only means every value is visited about twice in total, so the whole thing is O(n).

question.md:
A chain is `v, v + step, v + 2·step, …`. From the numbers you're given (each used at most once,
in any order), build the longest chain and return its length.

- **Order in the input doesn't matter.** You pick the numbers; you don't need them to be next to
  each other in the list.
- **Each number is used at most once**, and repeats don't help: `[2, 2, 2]` with step 5 gives
  chains of length 1, because 2 + 5 = 7 isn't there. Only *distinct* values matter.
- **Steps can be large and values negative.** `step` goes up to 10⁹ and values to ±10⁹, so
  `value + step` can reach 2 × 10⁹, beyond the 32-bit `int`. Use 64-bit arithmetic for it in
  Java, C++ and C.
- **Any single number is a chain of length 1**, so the answer is at least 1.
- **Size:** up to 10⁵ values.

think.md:
Take `values = [10, 4, 1, 7, 5, 13, 8, 2, 20, 23]` with `step = 3`.

By hand, you'd notice runs like 1, 4, 7, 10, 13. Every value belongs to exactly one maximal
chain (its next link is forced: `v + 3`; its previous link is forced: `v − 3`). Here the values
split into these chains:

think.caption: Shaded: each chain's head, the one value whose predecessor (value − 3) is missing.

think.md:
The key question is **where to start counting**. If you start at 7 you get 7, 10, 13 (length
3), which undercounts and wastes time. If you start only at values whose predecessor is
missing (1, 2 and 20 here), every chain is measured once and from its true start.

And "is the predecessor missing?" and "is the next link present?" are both membership
questions, which a hash set answers in O(1).

approaches.title: Extend a chain from every value

idea.md:
Treat every value as a possible first link. From `v`, look for `v + step` by scanning the
list; if it's there, look for `v + 2·step`, and so on. Keep the longest length found.

It's correct because the longest chain has some first value, and when the loop reaches
that value it walks the whole chain.

build: For each value `v`, set `length = 1` and `next = v + step`.
While `next` appears in the list (found by scanning), add 1 to `length` and move `next` up by `step`.
Keep the maximum `length` over all starting values.

lines.text: A plain linear search: is `x` anywhere in the list? It takes a 64-bit `x` because chain links can go past `int` range (a value of 10⁹ plus a step of 10⁹).
Every value gets a turn as the first link. The chain so far has length 1, and the link we want next is `v + step`.

notes.java: `(long) v + step` so the sum can't overflow.
notes.cpp: `(long long) v + step` so the sum can't overflow.
notes.c: `(long long)` so the sum can't overflow.

lines.text: While the next link exists, the chain grows by one and we look for the link after it.

notes.python: `in` on a list scans it from the start each time.

lines.text: Keep the longest chain seen from any start.

complexity.md:
**Time O(n³) in the worst case:** a chain of length n can be re-walked from each of its n
values, and each step of the walk scans n numbers.

**Space O(1).**

steps.text: Step 3. Try every value as the first link.
From 10: 10 → 13 (then 16 is missing). Length 2.
From 4: 4 → 7 → 10 → 13 (then 16 is missing). Length 4.
From 1: 1 → 4 → 7 → 10 → 13 (then 16 is missing). Length 5.
From 7: 7 → 10 → 13 (then 16 is missing). Length 3.
From 5: 5 → 8 (then 11 is missing). Length 2.
From 13: 13 (then 16 is missing). Length 1.
From 8: 8 (then 11 is missing). Length 1.
From 2: 2 → 5 → 8 (then 11 is missing). Length 3.
From 20: 20 → 23 (then 26 is missing). Length 2.
From 23: 23 (then 26 is missing). Length 1.
The longest chain has 5 links. Note how 4, 7, 10 and 13 each re-walked part of the chain that 1 already walked.

walk.title: Start a chain at every value and extend it as far as it goes.

limits.md:
Two kinds of waste. Each membership check scans the list (fixable with sorting or a set),
and each chain is walked again from every value inside it (fixable by starting only at
chain heads). The next approach removes the first waste, the best approach removes both.

approaches.title: Sort, then build chain lengths left to right

idea.md:
Sort the distinct values in increasing order. A chain that ends at `v` is a chain that ends
at `v − step`, plus `v`. Since `v − step < v`, that chain was already measured when we got
here. So:

`len(v) = len(v − step) + 1` if `v − step` is among the values, else `1`.

Finding `v − step` in the sorted list is a binary search, and the answer is the largest
`len` seen. No hashing is needed.

build: Sort the values and drop repeats.
Keep `len[i]`, the length of the chain ending at sorted position `i`.
For each `i`, binary-search `s[i] − step` among positions `0 … i − 1`. Found at `j`: `len[i] = len[j] + 1`. Not found: `len[i] = 1`.

lines.text: Comparator for `qsort` over 64-bit values, returning −1, 0 or 1.
Sorted distinct values, stored as 64-bit so `value − step` can be computed without overflow (it can go down to −2 × 10⁹).

notes.python: `set` drops repeats, `sorted` orders them. Python integers never overflow.
notes.java: The stream widens to `long`, sorts and removes repeats in one line.
notes.cpp: Copy into `long long`, sort, then `unique` + `erase` removes adjacent repeats.
notes.c: Copy into `long long`, sort, then compact the array in place keeping only the first of each run of equal values; `m` is the new length.

lines.text: `length[i]` will be the longest chain ending at `s[i]`. Every value alone is a chain of 1.
Left to right, so every smaller value is finished before it's needed.
Binary-search the predecessor link `s[i] − step` among the values to the left.

notes.java: `Arrays.binarySearch(s, 0, i, key)` returns the index when found and a negative number when not.
notes.cpp: `lower_bound` finds the first position not less than the key in `[0, i)`.
notes.c: A hand-written lower bound over `[0, i)`.

lines.text: If the predecessor exists, this value extends its chain by one; otherwise it starts a new chain (length stays 1).
The answer is the longest chain ending anywhere.

complexity.md:
**Time O(n log n):** the sort, plus one O(log n) binary search per value.

**Space O(n):** the sorted copy and the lengths.

steps.text: Sorted, without repeats: [1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 20, 23]. Process from left to right.
1: is -2 to the left? No, so 1 starts a chain of 1.
2: is -1 to the left? No, so 2 starts a chain of 1.
4: is 1 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 1, so 4 ends a chain of 2.
5: is 2 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 1, so 5 ends a chain of 2.
7: is 4 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 2, so 7 ends a chain of 3.
8: is 5 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 2, so 8 ends a chain of 3.
10: is 7 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 3, so 10 ends a chain of 4.
13: is 10 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 4, so 13 ends a chain of 5.
20: is 17 to the left? No, so 20 starts a chain of 1.
23: is 20 to the left? Yes, ending a chain of 1, so 23 ends a chain of 2.
The largest length is 5.

walk.title: Sort; each value's chain is one longer than the chain ending at value − step.

limits.md:
Fast and dependable, but the sort does more than needed: we only ever ask "is `v − step`
present?" and "is `v + step` present?", which a hash set answers in O(1) without ordering
anything.

approaches.title: Hash set, walking only from chain heads

idea.md:
Put all values in a hash set. For each distinct value `v`:

- If `v − step` is in the set, `v` is not a head: some chain reaches it from below. Skip it.
- Otherwise `v` is a head. Walk `v + step`, `v + 2·step`, … while they're in the set, and
  count the links.

Each value is the head of exactly one chain and is walked over only by that chain's walk,
so all the walks together take O(n) steps, even though there's a loop inside a loop.

build: Build a hash set of the values (64-bit keys in Java and C).
For each distinct value `v`: if `v − step` is in the set, skip it.
Otherwise walk forward from `v` while `x + step` is in the set, counting the links.

lines.text: C has no hash set, so these few lines build one. `slotOf` scrambles a key into a starting slot (multiply by a large odd constant, keep the well-mixed high bits). `has` walks forward from there until it finds the key or an empty slot; `add` walks the same way and claims the slot. With the table at most half full, each call is O(1) on average.
Every value goes into a hash set, so membership checks are O(1). Repeats collapse into one entry.

notes.java: `Long` keys, because we'll look up `v ± step`, which can leave `int` range.
notes.cpp: `long long` keys, because we'll look up `v ± step`, which can leave `int` range.
notes.c: A table at least twice the number of values, zeroed by `calloc`, then every value added.

lines.text: Consider each **distinct** value as a possible chain head. Looping over the set (not the input) matters: with many copies of a head, looping over the input would walk its chain once per copy.

notes.c: Walk the table's slots and skip the empty ones: the used slots are exactly the distinct values.

lines.text: If the value one step below is present, this value sits inside a longer chain. Its chain will be measured from the head, so skip it.
A head: count links upward until one is missing.

complexity.md:
**Time O(n) on average.** The skip test costs O(1) per value. A walk only starts at a
head and only steps through that head's own chain, and the chains don't overlap, so all
walks together take at most n steps.

**Space O(n)** for the set.

steps.text: All values go in a hash set.
10: 7 is in the set, so 10 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
4: 1 is in the set, so 4 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
1: -2 isn't in the set, so a chain starts here: 1 → 4 → 7 → 10 → 13, length 5.
7: 4 is in the set, so 7 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
5: 2 is in the set, so 5 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
13: 10 is in the set, so 13 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
8: 5 is in the set, so 8 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
2: -1 isn't in the set, so a chain starts here: 2 → 5 → 8, length 3.
20: 17 isn't in the set, so a chain starts here: 20 → 23, length 2.
23: 20 is in the set, so 23 is in the middle of a chain. Skip it; the chain's head will count it.
Each value was walked over at most once as part of a chain: best 5.

walk.title: Put every value in a set. Only walk from values that start a chain (value − step is missing).

takeaways.md:
- For "longest run of linked values" problems, **only start at the beginning of a run**: a value
  whose predecessor is missing. It turns a quadratic re-walk into a linear one.
- A loop inside a loop can still be O(n) when the inner loop's total work across all iterations is
  bounded. Count total work, not nesting depth.
- Sorting + binary search is a solid hash-free fallback: it costs a log factor.
